title: Same fact, different words
principle: The same fact feels different as a gain or a loss.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a test from 1981. Tversky and Kahneman asked people to imagine a disease that would kill 600 people. Plan A: 200 people will be saved. Plan B: maybe all 600 are saved (one chance in three), maybe none (two chances in three).

screens.title: Same plans, different words
screens.text: Then they asked a second group, using different words. Plan C: 400 people will die. Plan D: maybe no one dies (one chance in three), maybe all 600 die (two chances in three). Look. Plan C is the same as Plan A: 200 live, 400 die.

screens.prompt: 72 of every 100 people chose Plan A, "200 saved". How many chose Plan C, "400 will die"? It's the same plan.
screens.why: Only 22 of 100 chose Plan C. 78 chose the risky plan instead. The plan was the same. Only the words changed, from "saved" to "die".

screens.title: Framing
screens.text: Scientists call this framing. A gain frame says what you get: "200 saved". A loss frame says what you lose: "400 die". Same fact, different feeling. People choose differently, even when the facts are the same.

screens.title: It's used on you
screens.text: You see this every day. "90% fat-free" sounds healthy, but it means 10% fat. "Only ₹33 a day" for insurance sounds cheap, but it's about ₹12,000 a year. "Don't miss out!" is a loss frame. These words are not lies. They show only one side of the fact.

screens.prompt: Insurance costs ₹12,000 a year. An ad says "only ₹33 a day". Does it cost less?

options.label: No: it's the same price, shown per day
Can't tell without reading the whole policy

screens.why: Right. ₹33 × 365 days = about ₹12,000. Same price. Saying it per day only makes it feel small.

wrong.a: ₹33 is for one day. ₹33 × 365 days = about ₹12,000, the same as the yearly price. Only the words changed.
wrong.c: You can check with one sum: ₹33 × 365 days = about ₹12,000. It's the same price, shown per day.

screens.title: When to use each frame
screens.text: So which frame should you use? Here's my rule. For something new, use a gain frame: say what they get. If waiting costs them money every month, use a loss frame: show how much they lose by waiting. Only show a real loss.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: A disease test and your bakery seem very different, but words work the same way. It's April. You start a birthday cake plan for offices: a cake for every staff birthday, delivered that day, ₹850 each. Nearby offices buy from a chain shop at ₹1,100.

screens.prompt: A new office doesn't know you. Your sister says: "Save ₹250 a birthday cake." Your friend says: "You're wasting ₹250 on every cake!" Who's right?

options.label: Your sister: a gain frame for something new
Your friend: a loss always works better
Neither: send only the price list

screens.why: Yes. They have never bought from you, so tell them what they get. "You're wasting money" from someone new sounds rude, and people may say no.

wrong.b: A loss frame works for a cost they already know they pay. From someone new, "You're wasting money!" sounds rude. Tell a new office what they get.
wrong.c: A price list alone doesn't show the ₹250 saving. For someone new, a gain frame helps: "Save ₹250 on every birthday cake."

screens.prompt: A manager liked your plan last month but keeps saying "next month". They buy about 4 cakes a month at ₹1,100. Which message works best?
screens.why: Yes. 4 cakes × ₹250 = ₹1,000 a month. That loss is real, and they pay it now. Telling them this helps them decide.

wrong.a: There's no real deadline, so that message is false. Show the real loss instead: 4 cakes × ₹250 = about ₹1,000 a month.
wrong.b: They already know they can save, but they still wait. Showing the real loss helps more: 4 cakes × ₹250 = about ₹1,000 a month.

screens.setup: It's May. A big office wants all its birthday cakes for a year: about 48 cakes at ₹850 each, ₹40,800 in total. Each cake leaves you ₹450. You write the offer.
screens.question: How should you show the price?

options.label: "₹850 a cake, paid monthly. You save ₹250 a cake."
options.outcome: The manager sees each cake's price and the saving: about ₹12,000 a year. She signs. About 4 cakes a month, each leaving you ₹450: ₹1,800 a month, all year.
options.why: You used a gain frame for a new buyer, and the price was the same as the bill they'd get. Nothing would feel unfair later.

options.label: "₹40,800 for the year, paid now."
options.outcome: It's true, but the big number worries the manager. She says she'll think about it. Two weeks later, she agrees to six months only: 24 cakes, leaving you ₹10,800.
options.why: The price was correct, but it showed only the big number. She couldn't see the ₹250 she saves on every cake.
options.better: ₹850 a cake, paid monthly, with the ₹250 saving said plainly.

options.label: "Only ₹112 a day!" Yearly bill in small text
options.outcome: The manager agrees. Then her accounts team reads the small text: ₹40,800 due at once. They feel cheated and cancel. You lose the order, and they tell other offices.
options.why: ₹112 a day is about ₹40,800 a year, so it isn't a lie. But showing a daily price when the full bill is due at once feels unfair.
options.better: ₹850 a cake, paid monthly, with the ₹250 saving said plainly.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: The line again: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. Help buyers see the truth. Making a small problem sound scary puts pressure on people, and they say no. A daily price that hides a big bill feels unfair.
The same ___ feels different as a ___ or a loss.
screens.why: Correct. "200 saved" and "400 die" were the same plan. "Save ₹250 a cake" helps a new office buy from you.

summary: Framing: the same fact feels different as a gain ("200 saved") or a loss ("400 die").
"90% fat-free" and "only ₹33 a day" are frames. Look at the other side, or find the yearly price.
Use a gain frame for something new, and a loss frame only for a real cost they pay now. Never show only a daily price for a big bill.

cards.front: A gym says "only ₹25 a day". You must pay for the whole year at once. How much is that?
cards.back: ₹25 × 365 = about ₹9,000. Showing a daily price makes a big bill feel small.

cards.front: A new customer has never tried your tiffin. Which message is better?
options: "Hot lunch at your desk by 1 pm"
cards.back: For something new, use a gain frame: tell them what they get.

cards.front: "Yogurt: 95% fat-free." How much fat is in it?
cards.back: A frame shows one side of a fact. Look at the other side too.

sources.label: Tversky and Kahneman, The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice (Science, 1981)
